q.label: Semaglutide (Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy) and sudden vision loss (NAION)
q.hook: Europe and the UK now warn that semaglutide can, very rarely, cause sudden vision loss. The U.S. label doesn't.

EU.finding: PRAC concluded June 2025 that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide (~2-fold increased risk, ~1 extra case per 10,000 person-years); SmPC sections 4.4 and 4.8 and Package Leaflet updated

UK.finding: MHRA Drug Safety Update Feb 2026 agreed with European review recommendations to update product information but noted conflicting evidence in literature; 3 Yellow Card reports up to Aug 2025; product info updates pending

US_label.finding: Searched Ozempic v20 (2026-06-10), Wegovy v19 (2026-06-30), Rybelsus v14 (2026-08-19) — zero matches for NAION or related terms in any section

US_regulator.finding: FDA AEMS Q4 2024 (as of 2025-03-06) lists NAION as potential signal for GLP-1 receptor agonist class including semaglutide products; FDA evaluating need for regulatory action

why.sentence: The main reason is different_stage, because EU concluded and updated labeling in June 2025, UK agreed with EU review in February 2026 while noting conflicting evidence, and US FDA has only a class-level potential signal under evaluation since Q4 2024 with no label change.

reasons.claim: EU concluded and updated label Jun 2025; UK agreed Feb 2026 but noted conflicting evidence; US FDA still evaluating as class potential signal since Q4 2024

evidence.note: EU relied on epidemiological studies showing ~2-fold relative risk increase (~1 additional case per 10,000 person-years); UK referenced European review plus 3 spontaneous Yellow Card reports and noted conflicting literature; FDA uses AEMS/FAERS for GLP-1 class signal evaluation

recommendation.reason: EU and UK have concluded NAION risk warrants product information updates and clinical vigilance; US label lacks any mention but FDA is evaluating; hospital dispenses US semaglutide to 75 patients — in-house reminder and counseling at next dispensing is warranted now

items.text: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) Data from epidemiological studies indicates an increased risk for non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) during treatment with semaglutide. A sudden loss of vision should lead to ophthalmological examination and treatment with semaglutide should be discontinued if NAION is confirmed (see section 4.8).

q.label: Semaglutide (Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy) and sudden vision loss (NAION)
q.hook: Europe and the UK now warn that semaglutide can, very rarely, cause sudden vision loss. The U.S. label doesn't.

EU.finding: PRAC concluded June 2025 that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide; SmPC updated with warning in section 4.4 and adverse reaction in 4.8 with frequency very rare and excess risk ~1 per 10,000 person-years.

UK.finding: MHRA published Drug Safety Update February 2026 agreeing with European review recommendations; product information to be updated to include NAION risk; Yellow Card reports 3 cases since 2018.

US_label.finding: US labels for Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus searched (latest 2026) contain no mention of NAION, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or related terms.

US_regulator.finding: FDA AEMS Q4 2024 lists NAION as potential signal for GLP-1 receptor agonist class including semaglutide products; FDA evaluating need for regulatory action; Sentinel study on GLP-1 RA and NAION in progress.

hypotheses.name: eu_has_formal_nasion_signal
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC concluded June 2025 that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and recommended SmPC and package leaflet updates, implemented via worksharing variation.

hypotheses.name: uk_has_nasion_safety_update
hypotheses.why: MHRA published Drug Safety Update February 2026 agreeing with European review recommendations and stating product information will be updated to include NAION risk.

hypotheses.name: us_label_mentions_nasion
hypotheses.why: Full search of current US labels for Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus found no mention of NAION or related terms.

hypotheses.name: fda_has_nasion_potential_signal
hypotheses.why: FDA AEMS Q4 2024 lists NAION as a potential signal for the GLP-1 receptor agonist class including semaglutide products, with FDA evaluating need for regulatory action.

hypotheses.name: class_effect_assessment_differs
hypotheses.why: EU and UK assessed semaglutide specifically; FDA lists NAION for the entire GLP-1 class. Records do not clarify whether this difference drives the regulatory divergence.

hypotheses.name: evidence_base_or_causality_threshold_differs
hypotheses.why: EU cites several large epidemiological studies; UK notes conflicting evidence and few Yellow Card reports; FDA cites a single referral-center study and conflicting observational studies, with a Sentinel study underway. Records do not establish that different causality thresholds explain the divergence.

why.sentence: The main reason is different_stage, because EU PRAC concluded June 2025 and UK MHRA agreed February 2026 with label updates, while FDA lists NAION as a potential signal for the GLP-1 class and has a Sentinel study in progress.

reasons.claim: EU and UK have concluded reviews and updated product information while FDA is still evaluating the need for regulatory action.

evidence.note: EU relied on several large epidemiological studies showing ~2-fold increased risk (~1 extra case per 10,000 person-years); UK noted conflicting evidence in literature and only 3 Yellow Card reports; FDA cites a single referral-center study on semaglutide with subsequent conflicting observational studies, and has a Sentinel study underway for the GLP-1 class.

recommendation.reason: EU and UK have concluded NAION is a very rare risk with semaglutide and updated product information; US label lacks mention and FDA evaluation ongoing; in-house reminder and counseling at next dispensing aligns with EU/UK risk communication for 75 patients on semaglutide.

FDA Sentinel study on GLP-1 RA and NAION completes and results published
FDA AEMS potential signal list removes NAION or FDA takes regulatory action

UK.finding: MHRA published Drug Safety Update February 2026 agreeing with European review recommendations; product information to be updated to include NAION risk; Yellow Card reports 3 cases since 2018.

US_label.finding: US labels for Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus searched (latest 2026) contain no mention of NAION, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or related terms.

US_regulator.finding: FDA AEMS Q4 2024 lists NAION as potential signal for GLP-1 receptor agonist class including semaglutide products; FDA evaluating need for regulatory action; Sentinel study on GLP-1 RA and NAION in progress.

hypotheses.name: eu_has_formal_nasion_signal
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC concluded June 2025 that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and recommended SmPC and package leaflet updates, implemented via worksharing variation.

hypotheses.name: uk_has_nasion_safety_update
hypotheses.why: MHRA published Drug Safety Update February 2026 agreeing with European review recommendations and stating product information will be updated to include NAION risk.

hypotheses.name: us_label_mentions_nasion
hypotheses.why: Full search of current US labels for Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus found no mention of NAION or related terms.

hypotheses.name: fda_has_nasion_potential_signal
hypotheses.why: FDA AEMS Q4 2024 lists NAION as a potential signal for the GLP-1 receptor agonist class including semaglutide products, with FDA evaluating need for regulatory action.

hypotheses.name: class_effect_assessment_differs
hypotheses.why: EU and UK assessed semaglutide specifically; FDA lists NAION for the entire GLP-1 class. Records do not clarify whether this difference drives the regulatory divergence.

hypotheses.name: evidence_base_or_causality_threshold_differs
hypotheses.why: EU cites several large epidemiological studies; UK notes conflicting evidence and few Yellow Card reports; FDA cites a single referral-center study and conflicting observational studies, with a Sentinel study underway. Records do not establish that different causality thresholds explain the divergence.

why.sentence: The main reason is different_stage, because EU PRAC concluded June 2025 and UK MHRA agreed February 2026 with label updates, while FDA lists NAION as a potential signal for the GLP-1 class and has a Sentinel study in progress.

reasons.claim: EU and UK have concluded reviews and updated product information while FDA is still evaluating the need for regulatory action.

evidence.note: EU relied on several large epidemiological studies showing ~2-fold increased risk (~1 extra case per 10,000 person-years); UK noted conflicting evidence in literature and only 3 Yellow Card reports; FDA cites a single referral-center study on semaglutide with subsequent conflicting observational studies, and has a Sentinel study underway for the GLP-1 class.

recommendation.reason: EU and UK have concluded NAION is a very rare risk with semaglutide and updated product information; US label lacks mention and FDA evaluation ongoing; in-house reminder and counseling at next dispensing aligns with EU/UK risk communication for 75 patients on semaglutide.

FDA Sentinel study on GLP-1 RA and NAION completes and results published
FDA AEMS potential signal list removes NAION or FDA takes regulatory action

items.section: SmPC 4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use
items.text: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) Data from epidemiological studies indicates an increased risk for non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) during treatment with semaglutide. A sudden loss of vision should lead to ophthalmological examination and treatment with semaglutide should be discontinued if NAION is confirmed (see section 4.8).

q.label: Semaglutide (Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy) and sudden vision loss (NAION)
q.hook: Europe and the UK now warn that semaglutide can, very rarely, cause sudden vision loss. The U.S. label doesn't.

EU.finding: PRAC concluded June 2025 that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide; SmPC updated with warning in section 4.4 and adverse reaction in 4.8 with frequency very rare and excess risk ~1 per 10,000 person-years.

UK.finding: MHRA published Drug Safety Update February 2026 agreeing with European review recommendations; product information to be updated to include NAION risk; Yellow Card reports 3 cases since 2018.

US_label.finding: US labels for Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus searched (latest 2026) contain no mention of NAION, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or related terms.

US_regulator.finding: FDA AEMS Q4 2024 lists NAION as potential signal for GLP-1 receptor agonist class including semaglutide products; FDA evaluating need for regulatory action; Sentinel study on GLP-1 RA and NAION in progress.

hypotheses.name: eu_has_formal_nasion_signal
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC concluded June 2025 that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and recommended SmPC and package leaflet updates, implemented via worksharing variation. This is a regulatory conclusion, not an explanation for divergence.

hypotheses.name: uk_has_nasion_safety_update
hypotheses.why: MHRA published Drug Safety Update February 2026 agreeing with European review recommendations and stating product information will be updated to include NAION risk. This is a regulatory action, not a cause of divergence.

hypotheses.name: us_label_mentions_nasion
hypotheses.why: Full search of current US labels for Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus found no mention of NAION or related terms.

hypotheses.name: fda_has_nasion_potential_signal
hypotheses.why: FDA AEMS Q4 2024 lists NAION as a potential signal for the GLP-1 receptor agonist class including semaglutide products, with FDA evaluating need for regulatory action. This is a regulatory status, not an explanation for divergence.

hypotheses.name: class_effect_assessment_differs
hypotheses.why: EU and UK assessed semaglutide specifically; FDA lists NAION for the entire GLP-1 class. Records do not clarify whether this difference drives the regulatory divergence.

hypotheses.name: evidence_base_or_causality_threshold_differs
hypotheses.why: EU cites several large epidemiological studies; UK notes conflicting evidence and few Yellow Card reports; FDA cites a single referral-center study and conflicting observational studies, with a Sentinel study underway. Records do not establish that different causality thresholds explain the divergence.

why.sentence: The reason for the regulatory divergence is undetermined. EU and UK have concluded reviews and updated product information, while FDA lists NAION as a potential signal for the GLP-1 class and has a Sentinel study in progress. Open hypotheses H5 and H6 indicate that whether class-effect assessment or evidence-base differences drive the divergence is not established by the records.

evidence.note: EU relied on several large epidemiological studies showing ~2-fold increased risk (~1 extra case per 10,000 person-years); UK noted conflicting evidence in literature and only 3 Yellow Card reports; FDA cites a single referral-center study on semaglutide with subsequent conflicting observational studies, and has a Sentinel study underway for the GLP-1 class.

recommendation.reason: EU and UK have concluded NAION is a very rare risk with semaglutide and updated product information; US label lacks mention and FDA evaluation ongoing; in-house reminder and counseling at next dispensing aligns with EU/UK risk communication for 75 patients on semaglutide.

q.reaction: sexual dysfunction that persists after stopping the drug
q.label: Sertraline (Zoloft) and sexual dysfunction that persists after stopping
q.hook: Europe has warned since 2019 that sexual problems can continue after stopping SSRIs. In October 2026 the UK said it will add the term PSSD to patient leaflets.

EU.finding: PRAC recommended SmPC 4.4 and PIL updates for persistent sexual dysfunction after discontinuation in May 2019 based on EudraVigilance, literature, social media, and MAH cumulative reviews.

UK.finding: MHRA implemented new PIL measures in October 2026 including PSSD term, boxed warning, patient card, and ancillary leaflet after reviewing literature published since 2019.

US_label.finding: Zoloft v7 (2023-08-08) describes sexual dysfunction during use in Warnings and Precautions 5.11 and Adverse Reactions 6/6.1 but does not mention persistence after stopping.

US_regulator.finding: FDA AEMS potential signal lists 2023 Q1–2026 Q2 show no signal for sertraline/SSRI persistent sexual dysfunction; no label update for this risk.

hypotheses.why: EU PRAC recommended SmPC/PIL updates in 2019; UK MHRA implemented PIL measures in 2026; US label lacks equivalent warning.

hypotheses.name: different_evidence_threshold_for_causality
hypotheses.why: Records show EU considered EudraVigilance, literature, social media, MAH reviews; UK reviewed literature since 2019; US threshold not documented.

hypotheses.name: class_vs_product_specific_regulatory_action
hypotheses.why: EU and UK applied warnings at class level with product-specific PIL updates; US sertraline label only addresses sexual dysfunction during use.

hypotheses.name: divergent_postmarketing_surveillance_signal_detection
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC explicitly cited EudraVigilance signal detection; US FAERS quarterly lists 2023–2026 show no signal for sertraline persistent sexual dysfunction.

hypotheses.name: regulatory_framework_differences_precautionary_vs_certainty
hypotheses.why: No record explicitly states framework differences as cause; inference not directly supported.

why.sentence: The main reason is different evidence from postmarketing surveillance: EU's EudraVigilance detected a signal for persistent sexual dysfunction after sertraline withdrawal, while US FAERS did not reach a statistical signal threshold for the same outcome.

reasons.claim: EU PRAC acted on EudraVigilance signal detection; US FAERS quarterly lists show no such signal for sertraline persistent sexual dysfunction.

evidence.note: EU relied on EudraVigilance spontaneous reports, literature, social media, and MAH cumulative reviews; UK reviewed literature published since 2019; US FAERS quarterly signal lists show no detection for this outcome.

recommendation.reason: EU and UK regulators warn of persistent sexual dysfunction after stopping sertraline; US label only describes sexual dysfunction during use, so committee should add in-house counseling now.

FDA AEMS potential signal list includes sertraline or SSRI persistent sexual dysfunction

q.label: Sertraline (Zoloft) and sexual dysfunction that persists after stopping
q.hook: Europe has warned since 2019 that sexual problems can continue after stopping SSRIs. In October 2026 the UK said it will add the term PSSD to patient leaflets.

EU.finding: EU PRAC concluded in May 2019 that persistent sexual dysfunction after withdrawal warrants a product information update for SSRIs/SNRIs including sertraline, based on spontaneous reports, literature, social media, and MAH cumulative reviews.

UK.finding: UK MHRA concluded in October 2026 that the term 'Post SSRI Sexual Dysfunction' (PSSD) should be added to patient information leaflets for antidepressants associated with persistent sexual dysfunction, and issued a patient card and ancillary leaflet; the new boxed warning addresses suicidal thoughts and behaviours, not PSSD.

US_regulator.finding: FDA's quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) and Sentinel Initiative contain no signal for sertraline or SSRIs with persistent sexual dysfunction; no label update or safety communication has been issued.

state.askedText: The EU record covers a whole class (desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, escitalopram, fluoxetine…). Do the other U.S. labels in that class say it? Explanations that only restate the difference, not a cause of it: H1 (H1 "eu signal triggered label change uk us did not" (what wo …); H3 (H3 "class vs product specific regulatory action" (what would …). Judge them not_a_cause, or say what they explain. The Skeptic reads some records the other way round: H1: US-LABELS-SEARCHED is filed against it but shows it is the case; H1: SPL-Zoloft-v7-5.11-168d is filed against it but shows it is the case; H1: SPL-Zoloft-v7-6-ptsr is filed against it but shows it is the case; H1: SPL-Zoloft-v7-6.1-qxhq is filed against it but shows it is the case. If you agree, move the record and make the verdict follow it (an explanation a record shows true cannot be ruled out; one a record shows false cannot hold). Held partly on a search that found nothing: H4 divergent postmarketing surveillance signal detection. Not finding a record does not show a reason: judge it open, or cite a record that shows it. The why rests partly on a search that found nothing (FDA_POTENTIAL_SIGNAL_LISTS-NOTHING-FOUND). Not finding a record does not show a reason: cite a record that shows the reason, or, if no record does, make the why undetermined (where each regulator stands, and that the public records do not show why). The UK (MHRA) cell mentions a boxed warning, but its record says the boxed warning is about suicidal thoughts. Say what each measure is about, as the record does. H4 is incorrectly held on a search that found nothing; the main why (different_evidence) depends on this and should be undetermined. H1 and H3 are descriptive restatements, not causal explanations.

claims.why: All four records confirm PRAC's May 2019 conclusion that persistent sexual dysfunction after withdrawal warrants a product information update for SSRIs/SNRIs including sertraline, citing evidence from EudraVigilance, literature, social media, and MAH cumulative reviews.

The three UK records confirm MHRA's October 2026 decision to add 'PSSD' to PILs for relevant antidepressants, issue a patient card and ancillary leaflet, and that the new boxed warning addresses suicidal thoughts and behaviours, not PSSD.

The three label excerpts show sexual dysfunction described only during treatment (section 5.11 and 6.1), and the full-label search found zero mentions of persistent sexual dysfunction, post-SSRI sexual dysfunction, or PSSD.

The two records show no signal in FDA's quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) or Sentinel Initiative for sertraline/SSRIs with persistent sexual dysfunction, but they do not address whether a label update or safety communication has been issued.

The records demonstrate the regulatory difference (EU/UK action vs US inaction) but contain no information about the cause of that difference, so H1 merely describes the difference without explaining it.

EU-PRAC-REC-2019-05-01 shows the EU action was class-wide (all SSRIs/SNRIs), not product-specific; the other records do not show a cause for the difference, so H3 misstates the EU action and does not explain the cause.

explanations.why: EU records show a signal-triggered label change; UK records show the UK did add a PSSD term to PILs (contradicting 'UK did not'); US records show no persistent sexual dysfunction warning. The explanation simply restates the observed difference without providing a causal reason.

EU-PRAC-REC-2019-05-01 shows the EU action was class-wide (all SSRIs/SNRIs), not product-specific, so the record shows the explanation's claim about EU is false. UK-DSU-2026-10-15-04 shows UK action applied to antidepressants associated with risk (class-level), consistent with the explanation's UK side. The US label record is silent on whether the US evaluated at class level and found insufficient evidence.

state.askedText: The Skeptic reads some records the other way round: H1: UK-DSU-2026-10-15-01 is filed for it but shows it is not the case; H1: UK-DSU-2026-10-15-04 is filed for it but shows it is not the case; H1: SPL-Zoloft-v7-6-ptsr is filed against it but shows it is the case; H1: SPL-Zoloft-v7-6.1-qxhq is filed against it but shows it is the case; H1: US-LABELS-SEARCHED is filed against it but shows it is the case; H1: SPL-Zoloft-v7-5.11-168d is filed against it but shows it is the case; H3: EU-PRAC-REC-2019-05-01 is filed for it but shows it is not the case. If you agree, move the record and make the verdict follow it (an explanation a record shows true cannot be ruled out; one a record shows false cannot hold). Values outside the allowed lists: why type "unclear". Stage: concluded | agreed_with_noted_conflict | under_evaluation | no_public_action_found | not_found_in_sources. U.S. label status: written | partial | related_only | not found. Why type, one per reason: different_stage | different_evidence | different_scope | us_earlier | same_position (or undetermined, with no reason). Recommendation: propose | wait | no_action | already_covered. No explanation is judged to hold, yet the why gives a reason. If a record shows the reason, judge that explanation holds and name it the main cause; if no record does, make the why undetermined: say where each regulator stands and that the public records do not show why they differ. The why type must be 'undetermined' (not 'unclear'). Hypothesis verdicts must be 'holds', 'ruled_out', or 'open' — 'not_a_cause' is invalid. H1 and H3 lack records to rule them out; they should be 'open'.

claims.why: PRAC meeting minutes and recommendation document confirm May 2019 conclusion, evidence sources (EudraVigilance, literature, social media, MAH cumulative reviews), and inclusion of sertraline.
MHRA document from Oct 2026 states PSSD term added to PILs for relevant antidepressants, patient card and ancillary leaflet issued, and boxed warning addresses suicidal thoughts and behaviours.
Zoloft v7 label sections 5.11 and 6.1 describe sexual dysfunction during treatment; full-label search found zero mentions of persistent sexual dysfunction, post-SSRI sexual dysfunction, or PSSD.
FDA quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) and Sentinel Initiative searches returned no rows for sertraline or SSRIs with persistent sexual dysfunction.

q.reaction: sexual dysfunction that persists after stopping the drug
q.label: Sertraline (Zoloft) and sexual dysfunction that persists after stopping
q.hook: Europe has warned since 2019 that sexual problems can continue after stopping SSRIs. In October 2026 the UK said it will add the term PSSD to patient leaflets.

EU.finding: EU PRAC concluded in May 2019 that persistent sexual dysfunction after withdrawal warrants a product information update for SSRIs/SNRIs including sertraline, based on spontaneous reports, literature, social media, and MAH cumulative reviews.

UK.finding: UK MHRA concluded in October 2026 that the term 'Post SSRI Sexual Dysfunction' (PSSD) should be added to patient information leaflets for antidepressants associated with persistent sexual dysfunction, and issued a patient card and ancillary leaflet; the new boxed warning addresses suicidal thoughts and behaviours, not PSSD.

US_label.finding: Sertraline (Zoloft) U.S. label v7 (2023-08-08) includes sexual dysfunction in Warnings and Precautions (5.11) and Adverse Reactions (6.1) but describes symptoms during treatment only; a full-label search found no mention of persistent sexual dysfunction, post-SSRI sexual dysfunction, or PSSD.

US_regulator.finding: FDA's quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) and Sentinel Initiative contain no signal for sertraline or SSRIs with persistent sexual dysfunction.

hypotheses.name: eu_signal_triggered_label_change_uk_us_did_not
hypotheses.why: The hypothesis that the EU signal triggered a label change while the UK and US did not is incorrect because the UK has added PSSD term to PILs and issued a patient card.

hypotheses.name: different_evidence_threshold_for_causality
hypotheses.why: No record shows that UK/US required controlled epidemiological evidence; the evidence threshold difference remains unconfirmed.

hypotheses.name: class_vs_product_specific_regulatory_action
hypotheses.why: The EU action was class-wide for SSRIs/SNRIs, not product-specific; the UK action is also class-wide.

hypotheses.name: divergent_postmarketing_surveillance_signal_detection
hypotheses.why: No record confirms EudraVigilance detected a disproportionate signal for sertraline specifically, nor that FAERS/Sentinel failed to reach a threshold; the claim rests on a search that found nothing.

hypotheses.name: regulatory_framework_differences_precautionary_vs_certainty
hypotheses.why: No record addresses regulatory framework differences; the explanation is unsupported by the provided sources.

why.sentence: The public records show the EU and UK have added warnings for persistent sexual dysfunction after stopping antidepressants while the U.S. label for sertraline does not mention persistence, but the records do not reveal why the regulators differ.

evidence.note: EU relied on spontaneous reports (EudraVigilance), literature, social media, and MAH reviews; UK relied on a detailed review involving patients and families; U.S. surveillance (FAERS, Sentinel) did not detect a signal for this outcome.

recommendation.reason: The U.S. label for sertraline does not mention persistent sexual dysfunction, and the FDA has not issued a signal or label change; the committee should wait for a U.S. label update or FDA action before changing practice.

claims.why: All four records confirm PRAC's May 2019 recommendation to update product information for SSRIs/SNRIs including sertraline based on EudraVigilance, literature, social media, and MAH cumulative reviews, citing persistent sexual dysfunction after withdrawal.

Three UK MHRA records from October 2026 confirm addition of PSSD term to PILs, issuance of patient card and ancillary leaflet, and clarify the new boxed warning addresses suicidal thoughts/behaviours, not PSSD.
Three Zoloft v7 label excerpts show sexual dysfunction described only during treatment (section 5.11, 6.1, Table 4), and a full-label search found zero mentions of persistent/PSSD terms.
Two FDA search records confirm no signal for sertraline/SSRIs with persistent sexual dysfunction in quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) or Sentinel Initiative.
Records filed for show EU action and US inaction; records filed against show UK added PSSD term and patient card, confirming the hypothesis (EU acted, UK/US did not) is incorrect because UK did act.

Both records show EU action was class-wide (all SSRIs/SNRIs) and UK action is also class-wide (antidepressants associated with risk), supporting the draft's verdict that this explanation is ruled out as a differentiator.

explanations.why: The explanation merely restates the observed regulatory difference (EU acted, UK/US did not) rather than offering a causal mechanism; UK records contradict the 'UK did not' part.

The explanation posits EU action was product-specific and UK/US evaluated at class level with insufficient evidence; both records show the opposite (both actions are class-wide), so the explanation is false, not a restatement.

q.reaction: sexual dysfunction that persists after stopping the drug
q.label: Sertraline (Zoloft) and sexual dysfunction that persists after stopping
q.hook: Europe has warned since 2019 that sexual problems can continue after stopping SSRIs. In October 2026 the UK said it will add the term PSSD to patient leaflets.

EU.finding: EU PRAC concluded in May 2019 that persistent sexual dysfunction after withdrawal warrants a product information update for SSRIs/SNRIs including sertraline, based on spontaneous reports, literature, social media, and MAH cumulative reviews.

UK.finding: UK MHRA concluded in October 2026 that the term 'Post SSRI Sexual Dysfunction' (PSSD) should be added to patient information leaflets for antidepressants associated with persistent sexual dysfunction, and issued a patient card and ancillary leaflet; the new boxed warning addresses suicidal thoughts and behaviours, not PSSD.

US_label.finding: Sertraline (Zoloft) U.S. label v7 (2023-08-08) includes sexual dysfunction in Warnings and Precautions (5.11) and Adverse Reactions (6.1) but describes symptoms during treatment only; a full-label search found no mention of persistent sexual dysfunction, post-SSRI sexual dysfunction, or PSSD.

US_regulator.finding: FDA's quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) and Sentinel Initiative contain no signal for sertraline or SSRIs with persistent sexual dysfunction.

evidence.note: EU relied on spontaneous reports (EudraVigilance), literature, social media, and MAH reviews; UK relied on a detailed review involving patients and families; U.S. surveillance (FAERS, Sentinel) did not detect a signal for this outcome.

q.reaction: neurodevelopmental disorders in children of fathers treated with valproate
q.label: Valproate taken by fathers and neurodevelopmental disorders in their children
q.hook: Since 2024 Europe and the UK have told men taking valproate to use contraception, because of a possible risk to their children. In June 2026 PRAC re-reviewed newer, mixed studies: it kept those measures and asked for the product information to say the evidence is inconsistent.
q.note: first EU action January 2024 (CMDh endorsed PRAC's precautionary measures), UK Drug Safety Update 5 September 2024; the June 2026 PRAC entry in the night-scan ledger is a re-review

EU.finding: EU PRAC recommended precautionary measures for paternal valproate exposure in January 2024 based on a PASS registry study, and in June 2026 concluded evidence remains inconsistent but maintained the measures.

UK.finding: UK MHRA issued a Drug Safety Update in September 2024 advising contraception for men on valproate, after CHM review of the same PASS study.

US_label.finding: Depakote U.S. label v1621 (effective 2026-03-31) warns of neurodevelopmental disorders from maternal in utero exposure only; no mention of paternal exposure risk.

US_regulator.finding: FDA has not added a paternal exposure warning to the valproate label; FDA potential signal lists contain no entry for valproate and paternal neurodevelopmental disorders.

hypotheses.name: eu_acted_on_new_paternal_exposure_studies
hypotheses.why: UK MHRA reviewed the same PASS study cited by EU PRAC, so the claim that UK/US have not reviewed it is false.

hypotheses.name: uk_mhra_followed_eu_with_delay
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC issued precautionary measures in January 2024; UK MHRA issued its Drug Safety Update in September 2024, seven months later.

hypotheses.name: us_fda_awaits_stronger_causal_evidence
hypotheses.why: No FDA potential signal listing or public statement shows ongoing evaluation; absence of evidence is not evidence of awaiting.

hypotheses.name: us_fda_class_wide_review_pending
hypotheses.why: No record indicates a class-wide FDA review of paternal valproate exposure.

hypotheses.name: different_causality_thresholds_for_paternal_exposure
hypotheses.why: EU maintains precautionary measures despite uncertain causality; US label omits paternal exposure, but no record explicitly states differing thresholds.

why.sentence: The main reason is that regulators are at different stages: EU acted first in January 2024, UK followed in September 2024, and US has not yet acted on paternal exposure risk.

reasons.claim: EU acted first in January 2024, UK followed in September 2024, and US FDA has taken no public action on paternal exposure risk.

evidence.note: Regulators relied on retrospective observational registry studies (PASS study from Denmark, Norway, Sweden; Danish nationwide study); PRAC noted the evidence is inconsistent and the causal role of valproate is uncertain.

recommendation.reason: No patients currently on valproate at this hospital; U.S. label lacks paternal exposure warning; committee should monitor for FDA label update.

claims.why: Records show Jan 2024 PRAC precautionary measures and June 2026 PRAC conclusion that evidence remains inconsistent but measures maintained.
Records show UK MHRA Drug Safety Update Sep 2024 advising contraception after CHM review of the same retrospective observational study (PASS).
Label excerpts only discuss maternal in utero exposure risks; search finds no paternal exposure mention.
FDA signal lists show no valproate paternal neurodevelopmental disorder signal; label search shows no paternal warning.
Record shows UK MHRA reviewed the PASS study and CHM considered it, contradicting the claim that UK/US have not reviewed it.
Records show EU action Jan 2024 and UK action Sep 2024, confirming a delay.

explanations.why: Record shows UK MHRA reviewed the same PASS study, so the explanation that UK/US have not reviewed it is false.
Records show EU action Jan 2024 and UK action Sep 2024, confirming the delay; this explanation restates the temporal difference rather than providing a causal reason.

q.reaction: neurodevelopmental disorders in children of fathers treated with valproate
q.label: Valproate taken by fathers and neurodevelopmental disorders in their children
q.hook: Since 2024 Europe and the UK have told men taking valproate to use contraception, because of a possible risk to their children. In June 2026 PRAC re-reviewed newer, mixed studies: it kept those measures and asked for the product information to say the evidence is inconsistent.
q.note: first EU action January 2024 (CMDh endorsed PRAC's precautionary measures), UK Drug Safety Update 5 September 2024; the June 2026 PRAC entry in the night-scan ledger is a re-review

EU.finding: EU PRAC recommended updating product information for valproate regarding neurodevelopmental disorders with paternal exposure (June 2026), maintaining precautionary measures from January 2024.

UK.finding: UK MHRA issued Drug Safety Update September 2024 advising men on valproate to use effective contraception due to possible increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in children.

US_label.finding: U.S. label (Depakote v1621, effective 2026-03-31) warns of neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure only; no mention of paternal exposure risk.

US_regulator.finding: FDA has not issued labeling changes or public communications on paternal valproate exposure and neurodevelopmental disorders; potential signal lists and Sentinel show no active review.

why.sentence: Public records show EU and UK have issued precautionary measures for paternal valproate exposure while the U.S. label and FDA have not, but the records do not explain why the regulators differ.

evidence.note: EU and UK relied on a retrospective observational study using Nordic registry data (Norway, Denmark, Sweden) suggesting increased risk, but EU PRAC noted evidence is inconsistent with other studies not finding increased risk, and causal role remains uncertain.

recommendation.reason: Monitor for U.S. label update or FDA action on paternal exposure risk; hospital does not currently dispense valproate.

q.label: Valproate taken by fathers and neurodevelopmental disorders in their children
q.hook: Since 2024 Europe and the UK have told men taking valproate to use contraception, because of a possible risk to their children. In June 2026 PRAC re-reviewed newer, mixed studies: it kept those measures and asked for the product information to say the evidence is inconsistent.

q.reaction: neurodevelopmental disorders in children of fathers treated with valproate
q.label: Valproate taken by fathers and neurodevelopmental disorders in their children
q.hook: Since 2024 Europe and the UK have told men taking valproate to use contraception, because of a possible risk to their children. In June 2026 PRAC re-reviewed newer, mixed studies: it kept those measures and asked for the product information to say the evidence is inconsistent.
q.note: first EU action January 2024 (CMDh endorsed PRAC's precautionary measures), UK Drug Safety Update 5 September 2024; the June 2026 PRAC entry in the night-scan ledger is a re-review

EU.finding: EU PRAC recommended updating product information for valproate regarding neurodevelopmental disorders with paternal exposure (June 2026), maintaining precautionary measures from January 2024.

UK.finding: UK MHRA issued Drug Safety Update September 2024 advising men on valproate to use effective contraception due to possible increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in children.

US_label.finding: U.S. label (Depakote v1621, effective 2026-03-31) warns of neurodevelopmental disorders following in utero exposure only; no mention of paternal exposure risk.

US_regulator.finding: FDA has not issued labeling changes or public communications on paternal valproate exposure and neurodevelopmental disorders; U.S. label (Depakote v1621) does not mention paternal exposure risk.

hypotheses.name: uk_mhra_followed_eu_with_delay

why.sentence: Public records show EU and UK have issued precautionary measures for paternal valproate exposure while the U.S. label and FDA have not, but the records do not explain why the regulators differ.

evidence.note: EU and UK relied on a retrospective observational study using Nordic registry data (Norway, Denmark, Sweden) suggesting increased risk, but EU PRAC noted evidence is inconsistent with other studies not finding increased risk, and causal role remains uncertain.

state.askedText: The EU record covers a whole class (digoxin…). Do the other U.S. labels in that class say it? Values outside the allowed lists: why type "unclear". Stage: concluded | agreed_with_noted_conflict | under_evaluation | no_public_action_found | not_found_in_sources. U.S. label status: written | partial | related_only | not found. Why type, one per reason: different_stage | different_evidence | different_scope | us_earlier | same_position (or undetermined, with no reason). Recommendation: propose | wait | no_action | already_covered. Dates that the records each sentence cites do not contain: June 2025 (why sentence; it is in PRAC-R169, which it does not cite). Every date must come from a record the same sentence cites; do not estimate or predict. Ruled out only on a search that found nothing: H2 mhra issued dsu, H3 fda on potential signal list. Not finding a record is not a record against it: judge it open, or cite a record that rules it out. H2 and H3 incorrectly ruled_out based on search without result; must be open. Why type 'unclear' not allowed; use 'undetermined' with no reasons. Why sentence includes date 'June 2025' without citing PRAC-R169; either cite or omit date.

claims.why: PRAC-R169 explicitly states PRAC recommended an update of the EU product information for enzalutamide regarding digoxin assay interference at the 2-5 June 2025 meeting.
MHRA_DRUG_SAFETY_UPDATES-NOTHING-FOUND confirms a search found no MHRA Drug Safety Update article on enzalutamide-digoxin assay interference.

Both SPL-Xtandi-v24-5.8-103w and SPL-Xtandi-v24-7.3-u7yp show the digoxin immunoassay interference warning in sections 5.8 (Warnings and Precautions) and 7.3 (Drug Interactions) of the US label version 24.
FDA_POTENTIAL_SIGNAL_LISTS-NOTHING-FOUND confirms a search of FDA AEMS quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) found no entry for enzalutamide-digoxin assay interference.

The US label records (SPL-Xtandi-v24-5.8-103w, SPL-Xtandi-v24-7.3-u7yp) show the warning exists in the US label, which contradicts H1 (EU label updated only) and supports the draft's verdict that H1 is ruled out.
The US label records directly show the digoxin immunoassay interference warning in sections 5.8 and 7.3, confirming H4.

explanations.why: Both records show the US label contains the digoxin assay interference warning, which contradicts H1's assertion that only the EU label was updated (i.e., that the US label does not contain the warning). H1 is a specific hypothesis about the difference, not a mere restatement of the observed difference.

Both records confirm the US label includes the warning in sections 5.8 and 7.3, which is the factual basis for H4. H4 is offered as a causal explanation for why the FDA did not issue a signal (because the warning already exists), not merely a restatement of the regulatory difference.

q.reaction: Hallucinations, not related to serotoninergic syndrome
q.label: Vortioxetine (Trintellix) and Hallucinations, not related to serotoninergic syndrome

EU.finding: PRAC recommended updating EU product information for vortioxetine to include hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome (June 2025).

UK.finding: No MHRA Drug Safety Update mentions vortioxetine with hallucinations.

US_label.finding: US label includes hallucinations as a sign/symptom of serotonin syndrome (Section 5.2) and as a severe symptom of hyponatremia (Section 5.7), but does not list hallucinations unrelated to serotonin syndrome as a separate warning.

US_regulator.finding: FDA quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) do not list a signal for vortioxetine hallucinations unrelated to serotonin syndrome.

hypotheses.name: eu_specific_signal_detection
hypotheses.why: FDA potential signal list search found no signal, but absence is not evidence of no detection.

hypotheses.name: different_causality_assessment
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC recommends separate warning for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, while US label only includes hallucinations as part of serotonin syndrome.

hypotheses.name: regulatory_timing_lag
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC recommendation (June 2025) predates latest FDA potential signal list (2026 Q2), so timing lag does not explain difference.

hypotheses.name: class_vs_product_specific_action
hypotheses.why: Both EU and US actions are product-specific; no evidence of class-wide labeling for hallucinations.

why.sentence: The main reason is different causality assessment: EU treats hallucinations as a separate ADR, while US includes them only within serotonin syndrome.

reasons.claim: EU PRAC validated a signal for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, while US label subsumes hallucinations under serotonin syndrome, reflecting different causality assessments.

evidence.note: EU relied on PRAC signal evaluation (spontaneous reports, clinical data) recommending label update; US label based on clinical trials and postmarketing showing hallucinations as part of serotonin syndrome. No conflicting evidence noted.

recommendation.reason: EU warns of hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, but US label only mentions hallucinations within serotonin syndrome; in-house counseling can bridge the gap for 20 patients.

q.reaction: Hallucinations, not related to serotoninergic syndrome
q.label: Vortioxetine (Trintellix) and Hallucinations, not related to serotoninergic syndrome

EU.finding: EU PRAC recommended updating product information to include hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome as an adverse reaction (June 2025).

UK.finding: No MHRA Drug Safety Update on vortioxetine hallucinations found in available records.

US_label.finding: US label (v18, March 2025) lists hallucinations only as a symptom of serotonin syndrome (Section 5.2), not as a separate adverse reaction unrelated to serotonin syndrome.

US_regulator.finding: FDA quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) contain no signal for vortioxetine hallucinations unrelated to serotonin syndrome.

hypotheses.name: different_causality_assessment
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC concluded hallucinations can occur independently of serotonin syndrome and recommended a separate product information update, while US labeling only mentions hallucinations as a symptom of serotonin syndrome and does not include a separate warning for hallucinations unrelated to serotonin syndrome.

hypotheses.name: regulatory_timing_lag
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC recommendation (June 2025) preceded the latest FDA quarterly potential signal list (2026 Q2) which shows no signal, but FDA may still be evaluating; timing lag cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

hypotheses.name: class_vs_product_specific_action
hypotheses.why: Both EU PRAC recommendation and US labeling are product-specific for vortioxetine; no evidence that US regulators apply a class-wide labeling approach for this reaction.

why.sentence: The main reason is different causality assessment, because EU PRAC validated a signal for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome while US labeling only mentions hallucinations as part of serotonin syndrome.

reasons.claim: EU PRAC validated a signal for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, while US labeling only includes hallucinations within serotonin syndrome.

evidence.note: EU relied on PRAC signal evaluation (spontaneous reports, clinical data) recommending product information update; US label includes hallucinations only within serotonin syndrome based on class labeling; FDA signal detection has not identified a separate signal.

recommendation.reason: EU has a specific warning for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, but US label lacks this separate warning; the committee should add an in-house reminder and counseling at next dispensing.

reopen_when.text: US label adds a warning for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome.

claims.why: PRAC-R170 directly states PRAC recommended updating EU product information for hallucinations not related to serotoninergic syndrome for vortioxetine in June 2025.

MHRA_DRUG_SAFETY_UPDATES-NOTHING-FOUND shows no MHRA Drug Safety Update mentioning vortioxetine hallucinations; the retrieved updates concern antidepressants generally, suicidal thoughts, and sexual dysfunction.

SPL-Trintellix-v18-5.2-5lt4 lists hallucinations only as a symptom of serotonin syndrome in Section 5.2; US-LABELS-SEARCHED indicates no separate hallucination-related sections found in US label versions.
FDA_POTENTIAL_SIGNAL_LISTS-NOTHING-FOUND confirms no quarterly potential signal list entries for vortioxetine with hallucination terms from 2023 Q1 to 2026 Q2.

PRAC-R170 shows EU PRAC concluded hallucinations can occur independently of serotonin syndrome; SPL-Trintellix-v18-5.2-5lt4 shows US label only mentions hallucinations as a serotonin syndrome symptom, supporting the draft's verdict that different causality assessment is the main cause.

Both PRAC-R170 and SPL-Trintellix-v18-5.2-5lt4 describe product-specific actions for vortioxetine; no records indicate a class-wide US labeling approach for this reaction, consistent with the draft's judgement that this is not a cause.

explanations.why: PRAC-R170 shows EU treats hallucinations as independent of serotonin syndrome; SPL-Trintellix-v18-5.2-5lt4 shows US subsumes hallucinations under serotonin syndrome. Together they demonstrate divergent causality assessments, which is a causal explanation for the regulatory difference, not merely a restatement.

PRAC-R170 confirms EU action is product-specific. SPL-Trintellix-v18-5.2-5lt4 shows US labeling for vortioxetine is also product-specific, contradicting the explanation's premise that US regulators may apply class-wide labeling for this reaction. The explanation proposes a mechanism (class vs product-specific) that the records do not support, so it is not a cause and does not merely restate the difference.

q.reaction: Hallucinations, not related to serotoninergic syndrome
q.label: Vortioxetine (Trintellix) and Hallucinations, not related to serotoninergic syndrome

EU.finding: EU PRAC recommended updating product information to include hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome as an adverse reaction (June 2025).

UK.finding: MHRA Drug Safety Update search found no matching row for vortioxetine hallucinations; however, an independent check suggests a record (UK-DSU-2026-10-15-04) may exist but is not in the available records.

US_label.finding: US label (v18, March 2025) lists hallucinations only as a symptom of serotonin syndrome (Section 5.2), not as a separate adverse reaction unrelated to serotonin syndrome.

US_regulator.finding: FDA quarterly potential signal lists (2023 Q1–2026 Q2) contain no signal for vortioxetine hallucinations unrelated to serotonin syndrome.

hypotheses.name: eu_specific_signal_detection
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC validated a signal for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, but FDA potential signal lists do not contain this signal; the reason for the difference is not explained in the records.

hypotheses.name: different_causality_assessment
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC concluded hallucinations can occur independently of serotonin syndrome and recommended a separate product information update, while US labeling only mentions hallucinations as a symptom of serotonin syndrome and does not include a separate warning for hallucinations unrelated to serotonin syndrome.

hypotheses.name: regulatory_timing_lag
hypotheses.why: EU PRAC recommendation (June 2025) preceded the latest FDA quarterly potential signal list (2026 Q2) which shows no signal, but FDA may still be evaluating; timing lag cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

hypotheses.name: class_vs_product_specific_action
hypotheses.why: Both EU PRAC recommendation and US labeling are product-specific for vortioxetine; no evidence that US regulators apply a class-wide labeling approach for this reaction.

why.sentence: The main reason is different causality assessment, because EU PRAC validated a signal for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome while US labeling only mentions hallucinations as part of serotonin syndrome.

reasons.claim: EU PRAC validated a signal for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, while US labeling only includes hallucinations within serotonin syndrome.

evidence.note: EU relied on PRAC signal evaluation (spontaneous reports, clinical data) recommending product information update; US label includes hallucinations only within serotonin syndrome based on class labeling; FDA signal detection has not identified a separate signal.

recommendation.reason: EU has a specific warning for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome, but US label lacks this separate warning; the committee should add an in-house reminder and counseling at next dispensing.

reopen_when.text: US label adds a warning for hallucinations not related to serotonin syndrome.
